summary: Describes additional IPFIX Information Elements in the range 1-127, which is compatible with NetFlow version 9 field types, that were reused from Cisco. It builds on the IPFIX Information Model from RFC 7012.

eli5.summary: Network meters need names for things they count. This lists extra names that came from one company's older meter system.

questions: netflow v9 field types in ipfix
what is forwarding status in ipfix
subtitle: Standard names for flow export fields from Cisco networking equipment.

tldr.problem: Network flow export started with Cisco's NetFlow version 9, which used numbered field IDs. The newer IPFIX standard reused the same ID range for compatibility, but many NetFlow fields were never formally defined in IPFIX until now.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC formally registers 18 Cisco-specific IPFIX Information Elements in the range 1-127, which overlap with NetFlow version 9 field types. It covers sampling parameters, routing engine identification, forwarding status, and packet section data.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can continue using NetFlow v9 devices and IPFIX exporters with the same field numbers and clear definitions.

today: RFC 7270 is an Informational RFC that standardizes legacy NetFlow v9 fields to prevent confusion during migration to IPFIX. Network operators using NetFlow v9 exporters or collectors that support IPFIX continue to rely on these definitions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export) is the standard protocol for exporting flow data from routers and switches to collectors. NetFlow version 9, created by Cisco and published in RFC 3954, was IPFIX's predecessor. To ease migration, IPFIX reuses NetFlow v9 field IDs in the range 1-127.

However, when RFC 3954 was published in 2004, it did not document all NetFlow v9 field types. Many equipment vendors have continued using fields that were never formally registered. This creates confusion when deploying IPFIX: should collectors recognize these fields? This RFC resolves the question by formally registering 18 Cisco-defined elements in the IPFIX registry.
sections.eli5: Two systems count network traffic: the old Cisco system (NetFlow v9) and the new standard system (IPFIX). To make them work together, the new standard uses the same number IDs. But some old numbers were never officially defined, so this document defines them.

sections.title: What IPFIX Information Elements Are
sections.content:
An Information Element is a named field in a flow record. Each element has an ID number, a data type, and a semantic meaning. For example, element 1 is sourceIPv4Address, element 2 is destinationIPv4Address. When a router exports flow data, it sends the element ID followed by the value, so a collector knows what each number means.

IPFIX elements are grouped by their range: 1-127 are NetFlow v9-compatible, and 128 and above are standard IPFIX-only. This document focuses on elements 1-127 that were defined in NetFlow v9 but not yet registered in the IPFIX registry.
sections.eli5: Each field has a number. When the meter sends data, it says field 1 equals this value, field 2 equals that value. The collector looks up the number to know what it means.

sections.title: Sampling and Routing Information
sections.content:
Many IPFIX elements describe how a router sampled the flow or which engine processed it. samplingInterval (ID 34) is deprecated but was the packet-sampling rate (e.g., one of every 100 packets). samplingAlgorithm (ID 35) distinguishes deterministic from random sampling. engineType (ID 38) identifies the routing engine type in a Cisco router (RP, VIP, or PFC), and engineId (ID 39) identifies which physical slot.

Similarly, samplerId, samplerMode, and samplerRandomInterval describe the sampler configuration. classId (ID 51) and className (ID 100) map flows to QoS traffic classes. Many of these are deprecated in favor of newer IPFIX elements with more consistent semantics, but they remain for backward compatibility with NetFlow v9 systems.
sections.eli5: These fields say things like how many packets the meter looked at, which part of the router processed them, and which traffic class (fast or slow lane) the flow belonged to.

sections.title: Forwarding Status and Traffic Indices
sections.content:
forwardingStatus (ID 89) is a bitmap that encodes both the result of packet forwarding and the reason. The first two bits indicate whether the packet was Unknown, Forwarded, Dropped, or Consumed. The remaining bits provide detailed reasons: Forwarded packets may be Fragmented or Not Fragmented; Dropped packets may fail ACL checks, be Unroutable, have bad checksums, or many other causes; Consumed packets are punted to the CPU. This is one of the few Cisco elements still marked as current rather than deprecated.

srcTrafficIndex (ID 92) and dstTrafficIndex (ID 93) relate to BGP Policy Accounting, which associates flows with routing policy outcomes for accounting and traffic engineering.
sections.eli5: One field tells you whether the packet went through or got dropped, and why. Others link flows to routing policies so you can charge for them or understand where they went.

sections.title: Packet Data and Router-Specific Fields
sections.content:
layer2packetSectionOffset (ID 102), layer2packetSectionSize (ID 103), and layer2packetSectionData (ID 104) allow exporters to include a raw slice of a packet (for example, the Ethernet header). These are deprecated in favor of more generic packet section fields. Similarly, ipv4RouterSc (ID 43) is specific to Catalyst 5000/6000 switches and records the address of a router being shortcut during MultiLayer Switching. flagsAndSamplerId (ID 87) combines flow flags and the sampler ID in a single bitmapped field for internal collector use.

The RFC also reserves element ID ranges for other purposes: 65-69 for performance metrics (pending industry consolidation), 94-96 and 101 for application information, and 105-127 for other NetFlow v9 compatibility uses.
sections.eli5: A few fields are specific to Cisco hardware: they store raw packet bytes or internal router engine states. Most are old and have been replaced by standard versions.

items.label: Dropped
items.desc: Packet was dropped by ACL, routing, or hardware.

items.label: Consumed
items.desc: Packet was punted to CPU or consumed by switch.
